claims.text: The patient presented with a severe headache rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sudden 'thunderclap' onset after exertion, throbbing, diffuse, and associated with mild nausea but no vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, or neck stiffness.
The patient has no past medical history, takes no regular medications, and has no known allergies.

The patient lives alone, is independent in daily activities, works as a primary school teacher, engages in regular jogging, denies smoking or recreational drug use, and consumes approximately 6 units of alcohol per week.
Family history is negative for cerebrovascular accidents, aneurysms, migraines, or neurological conditions; the mother has type 2 diabetes and the father has hypertension.
Initial triage on 07/01/26 recorded blood pressure at 160/90 mmHg and heart rate at 88 bpm.

Initial neurological examination on 07/01/26 revealed no abnormalities, with the patient alert, oriented, and having intact cranial nerves, normal motor and sensory function, no focal deficits, and no neck stiffness.
A CT head scan performed on 07/01/26 showed no evidence of intracranial hemorrhage, mass lesion, or other abnormalities.
Blood tests collected on 07/01/26 showed mild leukocytosis (WBC 12.5 x 10^9/L), CRP 8 mg/L, and normal renal and liver function tests.
The patient was admitted to the Neurology ward with a diagnosis of Reversible Cerebral Vasoconstriction Syndrome (RCVS).
On 07/01/26, the headache persisted at 7/10 intensity, blood pressure was 150/92 mmHg, and blood tests showed mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) and marginally elevated CRP (12 mg/L).
MRI/MRA performed on 07/01/26 confirmed the diagnosis of RCVS.
On 08/01/26, headache severity reduced to 5/10, blood pressure was 135/85 mmHg, CRP was 12 mg/L, and mild hypokalemia (K+ 3.3 mmol/L) persisted.
On 09/01/26, headache severity reduced to 3/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and blood tests from 08/01/26 showed mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L).
On 10/01/26, headache severity reduced to 2/10, blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg, and mild hyponatremia (Na 132 mmol/L) was noted.
On 11/01/26, headache severity remained at 2/10, blood pressure was 125/78 mmHg, and a repeat MRA performed at 10:30 showed significant improvement in cerebral vasoconstriction.
On 12/01/26, the patient reported no further headaches, blood pressure was 130/80 mmHg, and the repeat MRA from 11/01/26 confirmed resolution of vasoconstriction.

Medication records conflict: Initial orders on 07/01/26 specified nimodipine 60 mg orally every 4 hours (note-5, note-6, note-7), while subsequent orders from 08/01/26 onwards specified nimodipine 30 mg orally every 4 hours (note-9, note-13, note-15, note-17).
Potassium chloride 1 g orally twice daily was prescribed on 07/01/26 and continued on 08/01/26 to correct hypokalemia.

Discharge medication records conflict: The ward plan on 12/01/26 listed nimodipine 30 mg PO QDS to be tapered over 2 weeks (note-17), while the GP communication on 12/01/26 listed amlodipine 5 mg OD (note-18).
The patient received education on RCVS, including avoiding triggers such as intense physical exertion, stress, triptans, and ergotamines, and was provided with a discharge planning booklet.
The rehab team assessed the patient on 09/01/26, noting mild residual neck stiffness but no significant functional impairments, and arranged for outpatient physiotherapy post-discharge.
The registrar contacted the GP on 07/01/26 to provide an update on admission and preliminary diagnosis.
The ward nurse contacted the GP on 12/01/26 to provide a summary of the hospital stay, discuss discharge medications, and confirm follow-up.
Discharge was planned for 12/01/26, with outpatient neurology follow-up arranged for 4 weeks post-discharge.
